chunks.content: A reasonably respectable speakeasy, smoke-filled, with quite a number of men and a few women leaning on the bar and seated around tables. Stew and Gallagher are seated at one of the round tables, smoking, drinks before them. Gallagher is reading a newspaper story, grinning as Stew mimics a woman’s voice: 'Mr. Smith, You wouldn't print that story, would you?' He laughs, saying he wouldn’t print it—only read it. Gallagher laughs over his shoulder at his imitation. She teases him, saying he’s going to be poison to that Junior Leaguer from now on. Stew replies he hopes not, since he has to call on her that morning. Gallagher looks up in astonishment, questioning his sanity. Stew insists the story is cold but he’s not—he’s sizzling. He demonstrates with a moistened finger touching his wrist, making a sizzle noise. Gallagher watches, quizzical, suspicious, and a little jealous. She draws out an 'O-o-oh!' as if realization has dawned. Stew, over her shoulder, declares that with the dawn came love, exclaiming that Gallagher must meet her because she’s 'it'—and he goes on enthusing about her qualities.

chunks.content: Stew continues rapturously, describing the woman as queenly, emphasizing that he knows queens, and praising her nose as 'the berries,' animatedly describing how she tosses it to the heavens. Gallagher dryly notes she doesn’t have a nose. Stew gives her a hurt look and insists she does, but distinguishes between types of women—like brewery horses and thoroughbreds. Gallagher deliberately misunderstands, pretending to defend the woman by saying she wouldn’t call her a brewery horse. Stew insists the woman is the real McCoy, and Gallagher retorts whether that makes the rest of them truck horses. Stew reproachfully tells her she’s talking like a woman. She responds with mild resentment, and he counters that while she’s his pal, she shouldn’t 'turn female' on him. Throughout this exchange, Gallagher watches him with a complex expression—she values their friendship but wishes he saw her as more than just one of the guys. Stew, sensing her attitude, grows slightly resentful and rises to leave.

document_metadata.title: 2、INT. SCHUYLER DINING ROOM
document_metadata.summary: Stew compliments the caviar, invites Mrs. Schuyler to visit, and exits with a bow, leaving her silently furious while Anne watches.

chunks.content: A lovely, sunny room with cretonne drapes and colorful painted furniture sets a warm, inviting atmosphere. Stew and Anne sit at a table, engaged in light, playful conversation. Anne appears amused and subtly intrigued, while Stew exudes the ease of someone completely at home. As he sweetens his tea from a modernistic, squatty little teapot, he reveals with dry humor that after years of research, he discovered he was the only man who hadn’t written a play—so now, in his spare time, he’s writing one. Though he admits he hasn’t figured out the plot, he shares that it’s set in a Siberian village. Anne teases him for his eccentricity, to which Stew denies any strangeness, claiming to be the most ordinary man—except for one flaw. When Anne guesses it’s that he doesn’t wear garters, he corrects her: he’s color blind. He explains that he’s been sitting across from her for half an hour and still can’t tell if her eyes are blue or violet. His candid, intimate observation catches Anne off guard, and she studies him with growing interest, remarking that something could be done with him. Stew leans into the moment, declaring himself malleable—'putty'—in her hands. He moves closer, asking permission to inspect her eyes more closely, and she consents with a teasing grace.

chunks.content: Stew gently takes her chin in his hand, studying her eyes up close as she smiles radiantly. He tells her to close both eyes, the moment growing warm and charged with unspoken tension. Just as the intimacy peaks, Mrs. Schuyler enters, stopping in the doorway, her expression a mix of stupefied indignation and fury. Anne quickly rises, caught off guard. Mrs. Schuyler, cold and commanding, declares that Stew’s idea to leave is excellent. Anne greets her mother, attempting to diffuse the situation, while Stew remains calm and polite, welcoming Mrs. Schuyler and offering her tea with hospitable ease. His nonchalance only deepens her rage. After a pause filled with tension, she demands to know what 'this person' is doing in her home. Before Anne can fully explain, Stew interjects, reiterating his earlier comment about trying to determine the color of Anne’s eyes. He turns to Mrs. Schuyler, asking for her opinion with feigned innocence. Mrs. Schuyler is on the verge of exploding, but Anne quickly pleads with her mother not to speak, insisting that Mr. Smith has come to do them a great favor.

A group of women nearby glance in Anne's direction, whispering among themselves. 'Say, who's Anne's new boyfriend?' one asks. Another replies, 'Well, if these old ears don't deceive me, I believe his name is Smith.' The first woman scoffs, 'Smith! Can't be one of the brothers—he hasn't a beard on.' Her companion quips, 'Well, he must have something if Anne has got her clutches on him.' At that moment, a piano chord rings out, shifting the focus of the gathering.Mrs. Baxter, the hostess, stands by the grand piano, where an anaemic-looking young man is seated. Beside her is a stout, swarthy Italian with bristling mustachios. She bows toward him, and he responds with a deep bow. Polite applause ripples through the crowd as some guests take their seats. Martini begins to sing, but unnoticed by the others, Stew and Anne quietly slip out of the room and into the roof garden.

document_metadata.title: 5、EXT. ROOF GARDEN
document_metadata.summary: Stew and Anne embrace on a divan, where he confesses his insecurities and feelings, she reassures him, and they share a passionate kiss, deepening their romantic connection under the intimate garden setting.

chunks.content: A most beautiful, romantic spot: rose trees in blossom, a vine-covered pergola, a splashing fountain, a few choice marble statues, and low, deep chairs arranged to create a gorgeous, intimate setting. Stew and Anne enter from the direction of the house, hand in hand, the garden dark except for the soft glow from the house’s interior. From within, a singer performs a deeply romantic, sentimental Italian love song, the melody lingering throughout the scene. They walk toward the edge of the pergola, where shadows deepen, drawn to a waterfall effect—a glass partition down which water gently trickles. They move behind the dimly lit fountain and settle into a low, deep divan, their figures seen in silhouette as they fall into a passionate embrace. The only sounds are the faint, distant voice of the singer and the continuous, soothing splash of water, creating a dreamlike atmosphere of intimacy and emotion.

chunks.content: CLOSEUP - ANNE & STEW on the divan, arms wrapped around each other. Stew, overwhelmed, whispers, 'Anne, pinch me, will you? Throw me out of here. Give me the air. Throw me out of this joint, will you?' Anne smiles, happy and serene, and gently pinches his nose. 'Why should I? We're happy, aren't we, darling?' she replies. Stew insists, 'Throw me out—because I'm beginning to get goofy ideas, and they concern you, Anne.' She responds passionately, 'None of your ideas can be goofy, Stew, if they concern me.' Struggling to articulate his feelings, Stew stumbles through a self-portrait: 'My name is Smith—that you’ve tolerated for a month. I'm white, male, over twenty-one, never in jail—not often, anyway. I prefer Scotch to Bourbon, hate carrots and peas, like black coffee, hate garters. I make seventy-five bucks a week, have eight hundred forty-seven in the bank—and I don't know yet whether your eyes are blue or violet.'Anne, still gazing at him intently, replies softly, 'That's because you're too far away, Stew,' even as he is close. Throughout his speech, her eyes never leave his. As he falters and turns, their eyes meet. His overwhelming desire for her surges, drowning out reason. He abandons his attempt at practicality, sweeps her into his arms, and kisses her passionately. FADE OUT: FADE IN

chunks.content: CLOSE SHOT - STEW Not knowing what it is all about, Stew, with an injured expression, takes the paper and looks at it. INSERT: Front page of Tribune ANN SCHUYLER ELOPES WITH REPORTER (with subheads giving more explicit information). MEDIUM SHOT The other reporters, copy readers, sob sisters, etc., seeing the unusual commotion and Stew's bewildered reaction, get out of their chairs and cross over to the City Desk, where they take up other copies of the same paper to look at. There are amazed and excited exclamations. CLOSER SHOT - STEW AND CONROY Stew, still staring dumbly at the paper. A few others are crowding around, glancing over his shoulder, etc. CONROY I've heard of people being scooped on their own funerals, but this! Holy mackerel! Why, it's news when Anne Schuyler gets her fingernails manicured, but this! She gets married to one of our own reporters and the Tribune beat us to it! (he notices other reporters milling around) Well! What do you guys want? Go on, get back to your desks. Go back to your work. (returning his attention to Stew) Now don't tell me you were drunk at the time and don't remember! Or is this one of Bingy's snow-storms? STEW No, no - it's true, all right, only we didn't want to get it in print yet, that's all. CONROY Why not? STEW Well, you see, I've acquired one of those new mother-in-laws, and we were afraid she wouldn't understand the whole idea. So we were going to wait till she went to Europe. CONROY What do I care about your mother-in-law! You're still working for this paper, aren't you! Or are you? STEW Yes, sir. CONROY Well, it's your business to get news! And here you had a story right in your own lap and you let the Tribune scoop us on it. Making a first class Grade A monkey out of me. If it ever happens again - just don't bother about coming back. That's all. He dismisses Stew with a wave of his hand. STEW Thanks for your congratulations.

document_metadata.title: 7、INT. JOE'S SPEAKEASY
document_metadata.summary: Stew insists he's lucky to be with Anne Schuyler and denies being trapped, despite inner doubt; he dismisses Conroy's mockery but remains troubled by the idea of a gilded cage.

chunks.content: Gallagher is seated alone at a table in the speakeasy, looking deeply forlorn, her life suddenly feeling empty. A drink sits untouched in front of her as she struggles to maintain emotional control. Stew enters the room, mingling with patrons who offer him congratulations. He eventually makes his way to her table, stopping to greet her with exaggerated cheer. She looks up, forcing a smile. Stew teases her for running away, to which she quietly replies that she didn’t. He pulls out the other chair and sits down, grinning boyishly, completely unaware of the emotional impact his recent actions have had on her. He presses her to congratulate him, and though it pains her, Gallagher sincerely wishes him all the luck in the world, placing her hand gently on his. Stew, warmed by her gesture, begins to open up, eager to share his excitement. He comments on her watery eyes, blaming the smoke when she deflects, and calls over the bartender for a drink. Brimming with pride, he marvels at how lucky he was to find a girl like Anne, pointing to a newspaper article about her, and insists Gallagher must meet her. She demurs, calling herself just an old load of hay, clearly distancing herself emotionally.

metadata.title: 7、INT. JOE'S SPEAKEASY
metadata.summary: Stew insists he's lucky to be with Anne Schuyler and denies being trapped, despite inner doubt; he dismisses Conroy's mockery but remains troubled by the idea of a gilded cage.

chunks.content: Stew, undeterred, suggests reviving their old tradition of spaghetti parties at her place, nostalgic for the carefree days of their friendship. Gallagher quietly notes they haven’t had one since he broke into high society. Stew, lost in fond memory, recalls the time he dropped spaghetti on the floor and served it anyway, laughing at the shared joke. He believes Anne would love such a story. Gallagher, with quiet skepticism, asks if he really thinks his wife—a Schuyler—would climb three flights of stairs to eat off paper plates. Stew insists she would, correcting Gallagher that it’s now Smith, not Schuyler. She murmurs an apology, but the correction stings. He offers to come alone if Anne won’t, but Gallagher firmly refuses, teasing that he’s a married man now and she’s been warned about such company. Stew grows resentful, accusing her of abandoning their friendship. She tries to brush it off, saying she’ll call him sometime, if his social duties allow. He cuts her off, insisting marriage shouldn’t change their bond. Just then, Gallagher’s expression shifts—she sees something that alarms her.

Conroy appears at the table and stops. He indicates Stew. CONROY: What's the Benedict[8] looking for in the newspaper - his lost freedom? Stew slowly sticks his head up over the top of the table, looking up. STEW (grinning sheepishly): Well, if it isn't old Fagin[9] himself. Conroy sits down at the table. STEW: Gallagher and myself just came over here to do a little work on a story - CONROY (disgustedly): Baloney! (calls off) Joe! Bring me a special! CLOSER THREE SHOT: Gallagher tries to be very bright and smiling. GALLAGHER (to Conroy): Isn't it swell about Stew's marriage? ? 41 ? CONROY (looking straight at her): Is it? Gallagher, self-conscious, realizes this tough old buzzard is on to her. She looks back at him for a moment - then drops her head. Stew is oblivious to this by-play. Conroy turns to Stew. CONROY: Well, when are you quitting? STEW: Quitting? I'm not thinking about quitting. Joe comes in with a drink for Conroy. CONROY: I take it you don't have to work for a living any more. He takes a sip of his drink and looks over meaningfully. CONROY: Mr. Schuyler. STEW (in a flash of anger): Now get this, Conroy. My name is Smith. Always was Smith - and always gonna be Smith. CONROY: Is that so? STEW: That's so.

chunks.content: CLOSE SHOT - STEW In bed, asleep, all curled up, his head on his arm. CAMERA TRUCKS BACK showing the magnificent bedroom, with carved wooden panellings, a raised, canopied bed. When the Camera gets to a point that takes in a LONG SHOT of the room, the door to the hall opens and a correctly attired valet appears. He closes the door noiselessly, goes over to the windows, and draws the brocaded drapes aside. Then he crosses to a covered object and with a small flourish removes the cover - revealing a birdcage. He approaches the bed. CLOSER SHOT As Dawson the valet stops beside the bed. The valet leans over and speaks distinctly. DAWSON Mr. Smith, sir There is no movement from the form on the bed. DAWSON Mr. Smith, sir! Still no response. The valet taps the bedclothes-shrouded shoulder gently. DAWSON Mr. Smith, sir Sleepily, Stew turns, his eyes heavy with sleep. MEDIUM SHOT DAWSON How do you like your bath, sir? STEW I like my bath all right. How do you like your bath? Stew peers up, puzzled. STEW Who are you? DAWSON (surprised) I'm your valet, sir. chunks.content: MEDIUM SHOT Stew stands in front of a mirror, fumbling with his dress tie. He pauses, his hands still on his tie. ANNE (reproachfully) Stewart! We're all waiting for you. Where's your valet? STEW I poisoned him. ANNE Stop trying to be funny, and get ready, will you? As he struggles with his collar, it springs off. STEW I'm not going! ANNE What are you talking about? STEW I'm talking about - I'm not going out. CLOSEUP - ANNE ANNE (controlling her anger) What am I going downstairs and tell those people? STEW Go downstairs, and tell them - anything. Tell them I'm not going. Tell them I'm not home. ANNE (getting angrier by the minute) Stewart, would you mind telling me why you're not going? CLOSEUP - STEW STEW Yes, I'll tell you - for the same reason I've never wanted to go out with those social parasites, those sweet-smelling fashion plates. I don't like them. They bore me. They give me the jitters. ANNE'S VOICE Do you know you're talking about my friends? STEW Yes, I'm talking about your friends, and they still give me the jitters. DOUBLE SHOT ANNE Well, are you going - or aren't you? Stew makes a move to embrace her. STEW Anne, come here. Listen ANNE (sternly - slipping away from him) Look out for my lipstick, Stewart. STEW I'll tell you what. Let's you and me sneak out all by ourselves ANNE (interrupting) Are you crazy? STEW Think of the fun we can have - we'll sneak down the back stairs and get in the valet's Ford. How's that? ANNE Will you stop being silly, Stewart? STEW (trying hard) I'll tell you what let's do - I'll take you and introduce you to all my gang. Would you like that? ANNE (hard) But I don't want to meet your gang.

chunks.content: It is many hours later in the drawing room, where the party is in full swing and the guests, including Smythe, are heavily intoxicated. In the entrance hall, a dice game is underway, while in the drawing room, a small group clusters around the piano, singing 'The Grasshopper Jumped Over Another Grasshopper's Back' with boisterous enthusiasm. The atmosphere is one of unrestrained revelry, signaling that the guests are having a grand time. Suddenly, the doorbell rings and a key turns in the lock, interrupting the merriment. The outer door begins to open, and a guest—glassy-eyed and clutching a whiskey bottle—staggers toward it. He attempts to block entry, declaring the event a private party, but Anne forcefully pushes the door open, causing him to fall. He remains on the floor, cradling the bottle, as Anne and her mother, Mrs. Schuyler, accompanied by Dexter Grayson, step inside, their expressions a mix of shock, horror, and disbelief at the chaotic scene before them.

Anne responds emotionally, 'Oh, Dexter!' At that moment, another guest emerges from the drawing room, feigning exaggerated politeness as he bows before them, further enraging Anne and her mother. They spot Smythe across the room, clearly drunk. Mrs. Schuyler demands the butler identify the intruders. Smythe stumbles over, grinning, and proudly announces they are his friends—'very lit-lit-literary people.' Grayson quietly confirms to Mrs. Schuyler that Smythe is drunk, to which she reacts with shock. Smythe confirms it with pride, boasting of 'double-strength' drinks. When she asks for Mr. Smith, Smythe dismisses the question with a jubilant 'Whoopee!' and exits, leaving Grayson to murmur in disbelief, 'Very, very drunk.'
